title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch was on the point of leaving when Korney came in to announce:
"Sergey Alexyevitch!"
"Who's Sergey Alexyevitch?" Stepan Arkadyevitch was beginning, but he caught himself at once.
"Ah, Seryozha!" he said out loud. "Sergey Alexyevitch! I thought it was the head of a department. Anna asked me to see him too," he thought.

And he recalled the timid, pleading expression with which Anna had said to him at parting, "Anyway, you'll see him. Find out exactly where he is, who's looking after him. And Stiva... if it were possible! Could it be possible?" Stepan Arkadyevitch knew what was meant by that "if it were possible" — if it were possible to work the divorce out so she could have her son.... Stepan Arkadyevitch saw now that it was no use dreaming about that, but he was still glad to see his nephew.
Alexey Alexandrovitch reminded his brother-in-law that they never spoke to the boy about his mother, and asked him not to mention a single word about her.

"He was very ill after that meeting with his mother, which we hadn't foreseen," Alexey Alexandrovitch said. "In fact, we feared for his life. But with proper treatment and sea-bathing in the summer, he got his strength back, and now, on the doctor's advice, I have let him go to school. And the companionship of school has certainly done him good. He's perfectly well, and making good progress."

"What a fine young fellow he's grown into! Not Seryozha anymore — fully Sergey Alexyevitch!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling, looking at the handsome, broad-shouldered boy in a blue jacket and long trousers who came in briskly and confidently. The boy looked healthy and good-natured. He bowed to his uncle as to a stranger, but recognizing him, he flushed and turned away quickly, as though offended and annoyed by something. He went up to his father and handed him a slip with the marks he had earned at school.
"Well, that's quite respectable," said his father. "You may go."
"He's thinner and taller — he's grown out of being a child and into being a boy. I like that," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Do you remember me?"
The boy glanced quickly back at his uncle.
"Yes, _mon oncle_," he answered, glancing at his father, and looked down again.
His uncle called him over and took his hand.
"Well, and how are you getting on?" he said, wanting to talk to him, and not knowing what to say.

The boy, blushing and giving no answer, carefully pulled his hand free. As soon as Stepan Arkadyevitch let go of his hand, he glanced uncertainly at his father, and like a bird set loose, darted out of the room.

A year had gone by since the last time Seryozha had seen his mother. Since then he'd heard nothing more about her. And in the course of that year he had started school and made friends with his schoolmates. The dreams and memories of his mother, which had made him ill after he had seen her, did not occupy his thoughts anymore. When they did come back, he deliberately pushed them away, treating them as shameful and girlish — beneath the dignity of a boy and a schoolboy. He knew that his father and his mother were separated by some quarrel, he knew that he had to stay with his father, and he tried to get used to the idea.

He disliked seeing his uncle, who looked so much like his mother, because it stirred up the very memories he was ashamed of. He disliked it all the more because, from a few words he had caught while waiting at the study door, and even more from the looks on his father's and his uncle's faces, he had guessed that they must have been talking about his mother. So, not to start condemning the father he lived with and depended on, and above all not to give in to sentimentality, which he considered so demeaning, Seryozha tried not to look at this uncle who had come to disturb his peace of mind, and not to think about what the uncle had brought up in him.

But when Stepan Arkadyevitch, coming out after him, caught sight of him on the stairs and called him over and asked how he spent his recess at school, Seryozha talked more freely with him, out of his father's presence.

"We have a railway now," he said in answer to his uncle's question. "It works like this, you see: two of us sit on a bench — those are the passengers — and one stands up straight on the bench. And we're all harnessed to it by our arms or our belts, and we run through all the rooms — the doors get left open in advance. Well, and it's pretty hard work being the conductor!"
"That's the one who stands?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked, smiling.
"Yes — and you need nerve for it, and quick wits, especially when they stop all of a sudden, or someone falls down."

"Yes, that must be a serious business," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, watching with a sad sort of interest those eager eyes, so like his mother's — not childish anymore, not entirely innocent now. And although he had promised Alexey Alexandrovitch not to talk about Anna, he couldn't hold himself back.
"Do you remember your mother?" he asked suddenly.

"No, I don't," Seryozha said quickly. He flushed crimson, and his face clouded over. And his uncle couldn't get anything more out of him. The tutor found his pupil on the stairs half an hour later, and for a long time couldn't tell whether the boy was sulking or crying.
"What's the matter? I expect you hurt yourself when you fell down?" the tutor said. "I told you it was a dangerous game. We'll have to mention it to the director."
"If I had hurt myself, no one would have known. That's for sure."
"Well, what is it then?"
"Leave me alone! Whether I remember or whether I don't — what business is it of his? Why should I have to remember? Leave me in peace!" he said, addressing not the tutor but the whole world.
